questions.question_text: Of the following parasomnias, which one is more common in females than males?
questions.explanation: No gender di!erence has been reported in sleepwalking, sleep terrors, orconfusional arousals. Nightmares are reported to be more common in females.REM sleep behaviour disorder is more common in males, particularly those overthe age of 50 years.Ref: Singh S et al. Parasomnias: a comprehensive review. Cureus. 2018 Dec;10(12).

questions.question_text: On corneal examination, Kayser-Fleischer rings are often present in patients with
questions.explanation: Wilson disease is a genetic disorder of copper metabolism that leads to copperaccumulation in various organs, primarily the liver and brain. The clinical symptomsare a result of organ dysfunction due to the direct or indirect e!ects of copperaccumulation. Wilson disease is typically described as a hepato-neurologicaldisease, with focus on signs of liver disease and extrapyramidal symptoms (e.g.wing-beating tremor and dystonia). Copper accumulates in multiple organs overthe course of the disease, leading to a variety of clinical manifestations, includingneurologic (40-50% at diagnosis), psychiatric (10-25% at diagnosis, and up to 100%over the disease course), ophthalmologic (Kayser-Fleischer rings and sunflowercataracts) and occasionally endocrinologic, cardiologic, or/or osteoskeletal. Kayser-Fleischer rings are green-blue corneal deposits.Ref: Litwin T et al. Psychiatric manifestations in Wilson's disease: possibilities anddi"culties for treatment. Therapeutic advances in psychopharmacology. 2018Jul;8(7):199-211.Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019Jul 30. p. 166.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is preserved in associative visual agnosia?
questions.explanation: Neurologic conditions such as strokes and other focal lesions have facilitated thedefinition of several disorders of visual perception. Apperceptive visual agnosia isthe inability to identify and draw items using visual cues, with preservation of othersensory modalities. It represents failure of transmission of information from thehigher visual sensory pathway to the association areas and is caused by bilaterallesions in the visual association areas. Associative visual agnosia is the inability toname or use objects despite the ability to draw them. It is caused by bilateralmedial occipitotemporal lesions and can occur along with other visual impairments.Ref: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition.2022. p. 927.

questions.question_text: Which of the following tremors is amplified as a target is reached?
questions.explanation: Ref: Crawford III PF, Zimmerman EE. Tremor: Sorting through the di!erentialdiagnosis. American family physician. 2018 Feb 1;97(3):180-6.

questions.question_text: A 76-year-old man is brought to the emergency unit by his wife. He had breakfastthat morning, but appeared unable to remember that he and his wife had planneda day out. He repeatedly enquired where she was taking him. She reports that heappeared bewildered, but was alert and had no sensory and motor deficitsthroughout. He returned to a normal mental state after 10 hours. What is the mostlikely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The fundamental clinical feature of transient global amnesia (TGA) is the acuteonset of amnesia. During an attack, patients cannot memorise or learn newinformation, that is, they have anterograde amnesia. They also cannot recallinformation acquired very recently, such as the events in the last several hours ordays (i.e., they also have retrograde amnesia). Most patients seem calm butbewildered. TGA lasts for 3 to 24 hours but is most severe during the initial 1-2hours. By definition, the total duration must not exceed 24 hours.Ref: Kaufman DM, Geyer HL, Milstein MJ, Rosengard JL. Kaufman's ClinicalNeurology for Psychiatrists, 9 Edition. 2023. p. 113.

questions.question_text: Which of the following drugs is contraindicated in angle closure glaucoma?
questions.explanation: Angle closure is the form of glaucoma that can be induced or worsened bypsychotropic medication. Topiramate has been associated with the development ofclosed-angle glaucoma, potentially due to swelling of the lens and ciliary body.Ref: Taylor DM, Gaughran F, Pillinger T. The Maudsley Practice Guidelines forPhysical Health Conditions in Psychiatry. 2021. p. 520.

questions.question_text: Which of the following drugs has the best available evidence for the treatment ofdepression following a myocardial infarction?
questions.explanation: Antidepressants are best avoided in the first 2 months following a myocardialinfarction. If clinically indicated, SSRIs (sertraline is the drug of choice; avoidfluvoxamine and citalopram/escitalopram) should be prescribed rather than TCAs.If sedation is required, consider use of mirtazapine or a small dose of trazodone atnight.Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 1033.

questions.question_text: What is the risk of depression in a cardiac patient with congestive heart failurecompared to the general population?
questions.explanation: Clinically significant depressive symptoms a!ect 21.5% of heart failure (HF)patients, with one-third of HF patients reporting elevated depressive symptoms onquestionnaires and 19% meeting criteria for a depressive disorder (typically majordepressive disorder, but some studies have included dysthymia and minordepression). These prevalence rates are similar in studies of inpatients andoutpatients, and they are approximately two-to-three times higher than the generalpopulation.Ref: Celano CM et al. Depression and anxiety in heart failure: a review. Harvardreview of psychiatry. 2018 Jul;26(4):175.

questions.question_text: The mean age of onset of chronic fatigue syndrome is between
questions.explanation: Chronic fatigue syndrome (CFS) predominantly a!ects adults, with a peak age ofonset between 20 and 45 years, and a female to male ratio of 3:1. The average ageof onset is 33 years, but CFS can develop in people as old as 77 years. Patients canbe ill for years or even decades. They most commonly report a fluctuating illnesspattern in which symptoms wax and wane but are always present.Ref: Cortes Rivera M et al. Myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome: acomprehensive review. Diagnostics. 2019 Sep;9(3):91.Bateman L et al. Myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome: essentials ofdiagnosis and management. In Mayo Clinic Proceedings 2021 Nov 1 (Vol. 96, No. 11,pp. 2861-2878).

questions.question_text: The ratio of prevalence of chronic fatigue syndrome in males compared to femalesis
questions.explanation: Chronic fatigue syndrome (CFS) predominantly a!ects adults, with a peak age ofonset between 20 and 45 years, and a male to female ratio of 1:3. The average ageof onset is 33 years, but CFS can develop in people as old as 77 years. Patients canbe ill for years or even decades. They most commonly report a fluctuating illnesspattern in which symptoms wax and wane but are always present.Ref: Cortes Rivera M et al. Myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome: acomprehensive review. Diagnostics. 2019 Sep;9(3):91.Bateman L et al. Myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome: essentials ofdiagnosis and management. In Mayo Clinic Proceedings 2021 Nov 1 (Vol. 96, No. 11,pp. 2861-2878).

questions.question_text: Diagnostic features of chronic fatigue syndrome include all of the following except:
questions.explanation: Myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS) is a debilitatingdisease with core symptoms of fatigue, unrefreshing sleep, post-exertional malaise,and cognitive dysfunction. The aetiology of the illness has yet to be revealed, whichhas led to no established objective diagnostics, pathophysiology, or therapeutics.Accordingly, many expert groups have developed case definitions based on clinicalfeatures. To date, over 20 ME/CFS case definitions have been established bydi!erent groups in various countries. The most widely used have been the Fukudacriteria and the international criteria.A case of ME/CFS is defined by the presence of an unexplained, persistent, andrelapsing chronic fatigue of new onset that is not alleviated by rest, which results ina significant reduction in the quality of life, and a concurrent occurrence of four ormore of the following eight symptoms that must have persisted during six or moreconsecutive months:1)     'Brain fog' – described as impairment in short-term memory or concentrationsevere enough to cause a reduction in previous levels of personal activities2)     Sore throat3)     Tender cervical or axillary nodes4)     Muscle pain5)     Multipoint pain without joint swelling6)     Headaches7)     Unrefreshing sleep8)     Post-exertional malaise lasting more than 24 hoursRef: Lim EJ, Son CG. Review of case definitions for myalgicencephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS). Journal of translationalmedicine. 2020 Dec;18(1):1-10.Cortes Rivera M et al. Myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome: acomprehensive review. Diagnostics. 2019 Sep;9(3):91.

questions.question_text: A 42-year-old woman has a history of 2 episodes of unilateral blindness that lastedfor few weeks. She now presents with paraesthesia of the left leg. An MRI showsmultiple demyelinating plaques. Which of the following is correct with respect toher illness?

options.text: It has a uniform, progressive course
It is due to a bacterial infection
It presents with diverse physical signs
It is more common in men than women
It occurs more commonly near the equator

correct_answer.text: It presents with diverse physical signs

correct_answers.text: It presents with diverse physical signs

questions.explanation: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an immune-mediated demyelinating disease. The cause isuncertain, but likely due to environmental factors (e.g. Epstein-Barr virus infection,vitamin D deficiency, latitude, and smoking) interacting with genetic predisposition.MS is twice as common in women as in men. It is seen with greater frequency asthe distance from the equator increases (i.e. in White populations living in northernlatitudes). It is characterized by multiple demyelinating lesions with a predilectionfor the optic nerves, cerebellum, brainstem, and spinal cord. MS is predominantly awhite matter disease. Diverse physical signs reflect the presence and distribution ofplaques. 85-90% of cases start with episode of acute neurological symptoms (e.g.optic neuritis). Most patients follow a relapsing-remitting course.Ref: Ron MA. The neuropsychiatry of multiple sclerosis. BJPsych Advances. 2018May;24(3):178-87.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not characteristic of chronic fatigue syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Chronic fatigue syndrome is a disabling clinical condition characterised byunexplained and persistent post-exertional fatigue accompanied by a variety ofsymptoms related to cognitive, immunological, endocrinological, and autonomicdysfunction. It is also characterised by a substantial reduction in previous levels ofoccupational, educational, social, and personal activities. Unemployment ratesamong those who su!er from CFS are between 35-69%.
Ref: Cortes Rivera M et al. Myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome: acomprehensive review. Diagnostics. 2019 Sep;9(3):91.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a feature of sleep terrors?

options.text: Vivid memory of dreams on waking up

questions.explanation: Sleep terrors are recurrent episodes of abrupt awakening from sleep characterisedby a panicky scream, with intense fear and autonomic arousal. The individualusually has no recall of the details of the event and is unresponsive to stimuli (e.gconversation) during the episode. Sleep terrors typically occur during the first thirdof the night, during slow-wave stage 3 of NREM sleep. Autonomic hyperactivity ismanifested by tachycardia, tachypnea, diaphoresis, flushed face, dilated pupils,agitation, tremulousness, and increased muscle tone. Episodes usually last for 5-10minutes.Ref: Leung AK et al. Sleep terrors: an updated review. Current pediatric reviews.2020 Aug 1;16(3):176-82.Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019Jul 30. p. 462.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is an example of subcortical dementia?
questions.explanation:
Cortical dementias consist of illnesses in which neuropsychologic signs of corticaldysfunction – typically aphasia, agnosia, and apraxia – accompany dementia.Because the brain's subcortical areas are relatively untouched, patients remainalert, attentive, and ambulatory. Alzheimer disease serves as the prime example ofa cortical dementia. In contrast, subcortical dementias are typified by a!ectivechange, and slowed mental processing, which overshadow cognitive impairment.Gait abnormalities constitute the other core feature. Prime examples are Parkinsondisease, NPH, HIV-associated dementia, vascular cognitive impairment, and MS.
Ref: Kaufman DM, Geyer HL, Milstein MJ, Rosengard JL. Kaufman's ClinicalNeurology for Psychiatrists, 9 Edition. 2023. p. 115.Shaik SS, Varma AR. Di!erentiating the dementias: a neurological approach.Progress in Neurology and Psychiatry. 2012 Jan;16(1):11-8.

questions.question_text: A 33-year-old woman has been referred by her dentist for a long history of facialtingling, numbness, nausea and temporomandibular joint pain. Her symptomshave been anatomically inconsistent, and the pain has tended to fluctuate. She hasinsisted on multiple investigations, which have shown no abnormalities. The mostlikely diagnosis is
questions.explanation: In ICD-11, bodily distress disorder has replaced the somatoform disorders of ICD-10. Bodily distress disorder is characterised by the presence of bodily symptomsthat are distressing to the individual and excessive attention toward the symptoms,which may be manifest by repeated contact with health care providers. Bodilysymptoms are persistent, being present on most days for at least several months.Typically, bodily distress disorder involves multiple bodily symptoms that may varyover time. Occasionally there is a single symptom – usually pain or fatigue – that isassociated with the other features of the disorder. The symptoms and associateddistress and preoccupation have at least some impact on the individual'sfunctioning.Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 867.International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems(11th ed. ICD-11; World Health Organization, 2020)

questions.question_text: A cognitive faculty commonly a!ected in patients with post-concussion syndromeis
questions.explanation: Attention deficits and impairment of processing speed are commonly seen in mildtraumatic brain injury and post-concussion syndrome. Situational factorscontributing to neuropsychological disability in these cases include rapidprocessing demands, need for complex cognitive attention, and externaldistractions.Ref: Broshek DK et al. A review of post-concussion syndrome and psychologicalfactors associated with concussion. Brain injury. 2015 Jan 28;29(2):228-37.Kaltiainen H et al. Mild traumatic brain injury a!ects cognitive processing andmodifies oscillatory brain activity during attentional tasks. Journal of Neurotrauma.2019 Jul 15;36(14):2222-32.

questions.question_text: Which of the following are commonly seen in patients with post-concussionsyndrome?

options.text: Short term memory loss and personality changes
Dizziness, headaches, irritability, and slowed information processing

correct_answer.text: Dizziness, headaches, irritability, and slowed information processing

correct_answers.text: Dizziness, headaches, irritability, and slowed information processing

questions.explanation: Post-concussion syndrome is characterised by one or more core symptoms –headache, memory impairment, and insomnia – lasting more than 2 to 3 monthsafter a head injury. These and other symptoms of post-concussion syndrome –including irritability, sleepiness, tinnitus – remain entirely subjective and oftennonspecific, variable, and occasionally unending. Patients with post-concussionsyndrome characteristically describe mild amnesia accompanied by inattention oreasy distractibility, slowed information processing, and di"culty completingcomplex mental tasks. Post-concussion syndrome patients also often reportdizziness. In most cases, the dizziness is not authentic vertigo, but a nonspecificsensation with variable, idiosyncratic meanings that substitutes forlightheadedness, anxiety, unsteadiness, or lassitude. Patients have a normalphysical and neurologic examination, CT, and MRI. Although the EEG may showminor abnormalities, the changes are generally inconsistent, insignificant, andoften attributable to medications.Ref: Kaufman DM, Geyer HL, Milstein MJ, Rosengard JL. Kaufman's ClinicalNeurology for Psychiatrists, 9 Edition. 2023. pp. 559-560.

questions.question_text: A geriatric patient had a stroke 8 months ago. He now presents with retardation,amotivation, and anhedonia. He does not have any tearfulness or guilt. His MMSEscore is 22/30 and he has executive dysfunction. What is his most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The vascular depression hypothesis postulates that cerebrovascular disease maypredispose, precipitate, or perpetuate some geriatric depressive syndromes.Neurological signs and/or neurological findings, usually executive dysfunction, arefound in most patients with vascular depression depending on the location andextent of lesions. Patients with vascular depression often present with retardation,anhedonia, lack of insight into their illness, and disability. They are less likely toreport feelings of guilt.Ref: Alexopoulos GS. Mechanisms and treatment of late-life depression.Translational psychiatry. 2019 Aug 5;9(1):188.

questions.question_text: A 29-year-old woman is 6 months pregnant. She is depressed, has a previoushistory of depression, and a family history of depression. She has responded wellto paroxetine in the past. If she were to take paroxetine for the remainder of herpregnancy, which of the following e!ects is most likely to be seen in the newborn?
questions.explanation: SSRIs do not appear to be major teratogens, with most data supporting the safetyof fluoxetine. When taken late in pregnancy, SSRIs may increase the risk ofpersistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn; the absolute risk is very low.Women who take SSRIs may be at increased risk of postpartum haemorrhage. Theneonate may experience discontinuation symptoms, which are usually mild (suchas agitation or irritability), or rarely respiratory distress and convulsions, with SSRIs.The risk is particularly high with short half-life drugs such as paroxetine andvenlafaxine.Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines inPsychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. pp. 685-689.

questions.question_text: As a member of the hospital consultation-liaison team, you decide to prescribe an anti-depressant for a 65-year-old man who has recently suffered a stroke whilst on warfarin. You are concerned about antidepressants interacting with warfarin, but want to prescribe the antidepressant that is best supported by the current evidence base. What will be your choice of medication?
questions.explanation: According to the Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines, SSRIs continue to be the mostpreferred, evidence-based class of drugs for post-stroke depression. If the indexstroke was haemorrhagic, we need to be cautious about SSRIs increasing the risk offurther haemorrhages, especially if the patient had to continue anticoagulation forother reasons. If the patient is taking warfarin or other oral anticoagulants, theguidelines suggest using citalopram or escitalopram as they probably have thelowest interaction potential with warfarin among all SSRIs and use the loweste!ective dose.Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines inPsychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 362.Mortensen JK, Andersen G. Pharmacological management of post-strokedepression: an update of the evidence and clinical guidance. Expert Opinion onPharmacotherapy. 2021 Jun 13;22(9):1157-66.

questions.question_text: Which of the following pregnant mothers has the highest risk of having a child withADHD?

options.text: 30 year old woman who drinks one glass of red wine a day
31 year old woman who drinks 3 mugs of co!ee a day
21 year old woman who smokes 12 cigarettes a day
26 year old woman who has no substance use habits
22 year old woman who smokes one joint of marijuana a day

correct_answer.text: 21 year old woman who smokes 12 cigarettes a day

correct_answers.text: 21 year old woman who smokes 12 cigarettes a day

questions.explanation: Maternal smoking during pregnancy is associated with an increased risk of ADHD inchildren. Maternal pre-pregnancy obesity and overweight, pre-eclampsia,hypertension, acetaminophen exposure, and smoking during pregnancy arestrongly associated with ADHD.Ref: He Y et al. Maternal smoking during pregnancy and ADHD: results from asystematic review and meta-analysis of prospective cohort studies. Journal ofattention disorders. 2020 Oct;24(12):1637-47.Kim JH et al. Environmental risk factors, protective factors, and peripheralbiomarkers for ADHD: an umbrella review. The Lancet Psychiatry. 2020 Nov1;7(11):955-70.

questions.question_text: A 21-year-old woman has been diagnosed with postpartum depression and iscurrently receiving antidepressant treatment. Which observer rating would be mostappropriate to use to assess her response to treatment?
questions.explanation: The Montgomery-Asberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRaS) is a 10-item observer-rated scale. Each item is rated 0-6, with a total score obtained. Response to anantidepressant is usually defined as a 50% or more decrease from baseline on theMADRaS, and remission is defined as a score of 10 or less. The Edinburgh PostnatalDepression Scale is a 10-item tool developed for screeningscreening postpartum women fordepression in outpatient clinics, home visits, or during postpartum appointments.Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 97.Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition.2022. p. 603.Smith-Nielsen J et al. Validation of the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scaleagainst both DSM-5 and ICD-10 diagnostic criteria for depression. BMC psychiatry.2018 Dec;18(1):1-2.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is correct with regard to the mechanism of action ofmodafinil?

options.text: It inhibits noradrenaline in the hypothalamus
It reduces dopamine in the nucleus accumbens
It activates neurons that release orexin

correct_answer.text: It activates neurons that release orexin

correct_answers.text: It activates neurons that release orexin

questions.explanation: Exactly how modafinil works is unknown, but it is clearly di!erent from classicalstimulants such as methylphenidate and amphetamine. Blockade of the dopaminetransporter (DAT) by modafinil leads to increased tonic dopaminergic firing anddownstream e!ects on wake-promoting neurotransmitters. Specifically, corticalrelease of wake-promoting neurotransmitters is increased, which leads todownstream release of histamine from the tuberomammillary nucleus and furtheractivation of the lateral hypothalamus, with corresponding orexin release thatstabilises wakefulness. Modafinil activates hypothalamic neurons that releaseorexin/hypocretin. The elimination half-life of modafinil is 10-12 hours.Ref: Stahl SM. Stahl's Essential Psychopharmacology: Prescriber's Guide, 7 Edition.2021. pp. 521-523.Stahl SM. Stahl's Essential Psychopharmacology: Neuroscientific Basis and PracticalApplications, 5 Edition. 2021. p. 445.

questions.question_text: Modafinil, which is used for daytime sleepiness, causes which of the followingneurochemical changes?
questions.explanation: Increased synaptic dopamine following blockade of the dopamine transmitter bymodafinil leads to increased tonic firing and downstream e!ects onneurotransmitters involved in wakefulness. Specifically, this leads to downstreamrelease of histamine from the tuberomammillary nucleus and further activation ofthe lateral hypothalamus, with corresponding orexin release that stabiliseswakefulness. Modafinil activates hypothalamic neurons that releaseorexin/hypocretin. The elimination half-life of modafinil is 10-12 hours.Ref: Stahl SM. Stahl's Essential Psychopharmacology: Neuroscientific Basis andPractical Applications, 5 Edition. 2021. pp. 444-445.Stahl SM. Stahl's Essential Psychopharmacology: Prescriber's Guide, 7 Edition.2021. pp. 521-523.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a common side e!ect of modafinil?
questions.explanation: Modafinil most commonly causes headache (dose-dependent). Other notable sidee!ects include anxiety, nervousness, insomnia, dry mouth, diarrhoea, nausea,anorexia, pharyngitis, rhinitis, hypertension, and palpitations. Modafinil can causeCNS e!ects similar to those caused by other CNS agents (e.g. changes in mood and,theoretically, activation of psychosis, mania, or suicidal ideation).Ref: Stahl SM. Stahl's Essential Psychopharmacology: Prescriber's Guide, 7 Edition.2021. pp. 522-523.

questions.question_text: Which of the following antidepressants has an e!ect in common with anti-nauseadrugs such as ondansetron?
questions.explanation: Mirtazapine has 5HT3 antagonism action. The 5HT3 receptors best known toclinicians are perhaps those localised in the chemoreceptor trigger zone of thebrainstem - where they mediate nausea and vomiting, especially in response tocancer chemotherapy - and also those localised in the gastrointestinal tract itself -where they mediate nausea, vomiting, and diarrhoea/bowel motility whenstimulated by serotonin. Blocking these 5HT3 receptors can therefore protectagainst chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting as well as against serotonin-induced gastrointestinal side e!ects that can accompany agents that increaseserotonin. Oral disintegrating tablets of mirtazapine have been used peri-operatively for nausea.Ref: Stahl SM. Stahl's Essential Psychopharmacology: Neuroscientific Basis andPractical Applications, 5 Edition. 2021. pp. 309-311.Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines inPsychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 891.

questions.question_text: A 30-year-old woman with a history of bipolar disorder is currently breastfeedingher child. She develops mania, though the presentation is not severe enough towarrant hospitalisation. Of the following, which medication should be used for thetreatment of mania while she is breastfeeding?
questions.explanation:
Valproate and carbamazepine should be avoided in women of childbearing age.Women taking lithium should be advised against breastfeeding. Infants may bemore susceptible to dehydration and lithium toxicity, owing to immature renalfunction. When initiating a mood stabiliser postpartum, a mood-stabilisingantipsychotic, such as olanzapine or quetiapine, should be considered.
Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 1031.Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines inPsychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 703.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a characteristic sign of hepatic encephalopathy?
questions.explanation:
Patients with hepatic encephalopathy have asterixis. Asterixis can be elicited byhaving patients extend their arms and hands as though they were stopping trac.Their hands intermittently quickly fall forward and slowly return, as though flappingor waving good-bye.
Ref: Kaufman DM, Geyer HL, Milstein MJ, Rosengard JL. Kaufman's ClinicalNeurology for Psychiatrists, 9 Edition. 2023. pp. 136-137.

questions.question_text: A 35-year-old woman is brought for urgent assessment by her husband. He reportsthat she seems to be hearing voices and 'seeing things', and that her mood hasbeen unstable. She has no insight into these mental status changes but isconcerned about a rash on her face. Her husband also reports that she might havehad a seizure the other day, but she refused to come for assessment. Of thefollowing, what is her most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The multisystem autoimmune disorder systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is mostcommon in women in their 30s. Neuropsychiatric symptoms are common. Seizures,cranial nerve palsies, peripheral neuropathy, 'spinal stroke', and other focal signsmay occur, in addition to the common dermatological, rheumatological,haematological, and cardiovascular manifestation of the disorder. Depression andanxiety disorders are very common in patients with SLE. Psychosis is a raremanifestation, the most common being secondary to glucocorticoid treatment.Psychosis usually precedes or occurs early in the evolution of the disease, isassociated with lupus activity, and usually has a good prognosis after treatment.Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. pp. 150-151.Carrión-Barberà I et al. Neuropsychiatric involvement in systemic lupuserythematosus: a review. Autoimmunity Reviews. 2021 Apr 1;20(4):102780.

questions.question_text: Which of the following psychotherapeutic interventions does not have anestablished evidence base in HIV-associated depression?
questions.explanation: Several studies of individual and group psychotherapy for HIV-associateddepression have found a greater reduction in depression scores (particularly inMDD), improvement of immune status, and reduction of viral load when comparedto waitlist or supportive interventions in depressed seropositive patients. Individualor group psychotherapeutic programs for the treatment of HIV-associateddepression typically utilise cognitive-behavioural therapy (CBT) and/orinterpersonal therapy (IPT) techniques, including cognitive restructuring,behavioural activation and modification, emotional awareness, assertivenesstraining, stress management, and encouragement of socialisation. For patients withcomorbid personality disorders or traits, dialectical behavioural therapy (DBT) mayalso be particularly useful in enhancing coping mechanisms. Telehealthinterventions of several modalities, including CBT and IPT, have been shown toreduce depressive symptoms in HIV-associated depression.Ref: Medeiros GC et al. Depressive disorders in HIV/AIDS: a clinically focusednarrative review. Harvard review of psychiatry. 2020 May 1;28(3):146-58.Mendez NA et al. Interventions addressing depression and HIV-related outcomes inpeople with HIV. Current HIV/AIDS Reports. 2021 Aug;18(4):377-90.

questions.question_text: A 68-year-old man with a history of stroke now presents with right-sided droopingof the mouth and flattening of the right nasolabial fold. He is able to furrow hisforehead and close both of his eyes. What is the likely cause of the lesion?
questions.explanation: The facial nerves supply the 'muscles of facial expression'. Each facial nervesupplies its ipsilateral temporalis, orbicularis oculi, and orbicularis oris muscles –muscles responsible for a frown, raised eyebrows, wink, smile, and grimace. In aunique and potentially confusing arrangement in their neuroanatomy, eachcerebral hemisphere innervates both the contralateral and ipsilateral facial nervemotor nuclei. In the classical explanation, because of their crossed and uncrossedsupply, both cerebral hemispheres innervate the upper facial muscles, but only thecontralateral cerebral hemisphere innervates the lower facial muscles. Facial nerveinjuries cause ipsilateral paresis of both upper and lower face muscles. This patternis termed a 'peripheral facial' or 'lower motor neuron' weakness. In contrast, injuriesof the cerebral cortex or upper brainstem, which interrupt the corticobulbar tract,cause paresis of only the lower contralateral face. This pattern is termed a 'central'or 'upper motor neuron' weakness.Ref: Kaufman DM, Geyer HL, Milstein MJ, Rosengard JL. Kaufman's ClinicalNeurology for Psychiatrists, 9 Edition. 2023. pp. 33-35.

questions.question_text: In which of the following neurological conditions is anaemia a common finding?
questions.explanation: Subacute combined degeneration is a demyelinated disease commonly associatedwith vitamin B12 deficiency. It is commonly accompanied by anaemia.Ref: Cao J, Su ZY, Xu SB, Liu CC. Subacute combined degeneration: a retrospectivestudy of 68 cases with short-term follow-up. European Neurology. 2018;79(5-6):247-55.

questions.question_text: The prevalence of co-morbid depression in those with coronary heart disease is approximately
questions.explanation: The prevalence of depression is significantly higher in patients with coronary heartdisease (CHD). More than 20% of patients with CHD are depressed, with the risk ofdepression highest in those with more severe CHD. CHD patients with depressionare at increased risk for recurrent cardiovascular events and mortality.Ref: De Hert M et al. The intriguing relationship between coronary heart diseaseand mental disorders. Dialogues in clinical neuroscience. 2018 Mar;20(1):31.

questions.question_text: Compared to the general population, suicide rates in patients with Huntingtondisease are
questions.explanation: Suicidal ideation/attempts are common in Huntington disease. Rates of suicide areapproximately 4 times higher than the general population. Risk of suicide iscorrelated with family history of suicide, history of previous attempts, and presenceof depression, especially in prodromal stages.Ref: Bachoud-Lévi AC et al. International Guidelines for the treatment ofHuntington's Disease. Frontiers in neurology. 2019;10:710.Kachian ZR et al. Suicidal ideation and behavior in Huntington's disease: Systematicreview and recommendations. Journal of a!ective disorders. 2019 May 1;250:319-29.

questions.question_text: Amnesia is commonly seen in the setting of
questions.explanation: Herpes simplex encephalitis causes amnesia accompanied by personality changes,focal impaired awareness seizures (previously named complex partial seizures),and the Kluver-Bucy syndrome because the virus typically enters the undersurfaceof the brain through the nasopharynx and preferentially attacks the temporallobes. This condition occurs relatively frequently because herpes simplex is themost common cause of sporadically occurring (non-epidemic) viral encephalitis. In contrast, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) encephalitis does not cause thispicture.Ref: Kaufman DM, Geyer HL, Milstein MJ, Rosengard JL. Kaufman's ClinicalNeurology for Psychiatrists, 9 Edition. 2023. p. 112.

questions.question_text: Which of the following occurs in Ganser syndrome?
questions.explanation: Ganser syndrome is characterised by approximate answers, disorientation,clouding of consciousness, hallucinations/pseudo-hallucinations, motordisturbance, anxiety or apathy, normal ADLs, and sudden resolution with amnesiafor the period of illness. In ICD-11, it is included under 'other specified dissociativedisorders'.Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 236.Dieguez S. Ganser syndrome. Neurologic-Psychiatric Syndromes in Focus-Part II.2018;42:1-22.

questions.question_text: A patient with bipolar disorder and a history of mixed affective states is in the first trimester of her pregnancy. She has not been on any medications of late, but is very concerned about the possibility of relapse. Of the following, what would bethe preferred medication to prescribe to her?
questions.explanation: For pregnant women with bipolar disorder who have had a long period withoutrelapse, the possibility of switching to a safer drug (antipsychotic) or withdrawingtreatment completely before conception and for at least the first trimester shouldbe considered. No mood stabiliser is clearly safe. NICE recommends the use ofmood stabilising antipsychotics as a preferable alternative to a mood stabiliser.Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines inPsychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 692.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following medications could be used to treat pathologic crying?
questions.explanation: The most conspicuous feature of pseudobulbar palsy is emotional lability. With littleor no provocation, patients tend to burst into tears or, less often, laughter, with noapparent change in their mood. These unprovoked emotional expressions arereferred to as pathologic laughing and crying, pseudobulbar a!ect, or involuntaryemotional expression disorder. Amitriptyline, SSRIs (such as citalopram), or acombination of dextromethorphan and quinidine may suppress this.Ref: Kaufman DM, Geyer HL, Milstein MJ, Rosengard JL. Kaufman's ClinicalNeurology for Psychiatrists, 9 Edition. 2023. p. 39.

questions.question_text: A pregnant bipolar patient has no other treatment option but to continue valproate. Which of the following should she take in addition?
questions.explanation: Valproate is an established human teratogen. Usually, valproate should be reservedfor post-menopausal women only. Its use in younger women should be treatmentof last resort. There is no evidence that folate protects against anticonvulsant-induced neural tube defects if given during pregnancy, but may do so if given priorto conception (the neural tube is essentially formed by 8 weeks of pregnancybefore many women realise they are pregnant). However, folate supplementationmay be beneficial for early neurodevelopment and so should always be o!ered.Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines inPsychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. pp. 260, 680, 691.

questions.question_text: Which of the following would be the most appropriate medication to prescribe for a pregnant woman with first-episode depression?
questions.explanation:
If initiating an antidepressant during pregnancy, previous response to treatmentmust be taken into account (i.e. consider using previously e!ective treatment). Forpreviously untreated patients, consider sertraline (least placental exposure). Whentaken in late pregnancy, SSRIs may increase risk of persistent pulmonaryhypertension the newborn, though the absolute risk is very low. The risk withsertraline may be lower than with other SSRIs. Neonates may experiencediscontinuation symptoms, usually mild, with SSRIs. The risk is particularly high withshort half-life drugs such as paroxetine and venlafaxine.
Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines inPsychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. pp. 687-689.

questions.question_text: Which of the following favours psychogenic nonepileptic seizures rather than epileptic seizures?
questions.explanation:
Ictal eye closure has been assessed in several controlled studies and is significantlymore frequent in psychogenic nonepileptic seizures (PNES) than epileptic seizures(ES). Closed eyes during an attack is considered a discriminator between PNES andES. The mean duration of PNES is longer than ES. There is considerable evidence tosuggest that a duration of more than 2 minutes is highly suggestive of PNES,although this is an arbitrary limit. Duration of longer than 10 minutes stronglysuggests PNES. In studies that have compared convulsive PNES with generalisedtonic clonic seizures, the proportion of events with side-to-side head or bodymovement, especially with coordinated agonist and antagonist activity, aresignificantly higher in PNES.
Ref: Xiang X et al. Di!erential diagnosis between epileptic seizures and psychogenicnonepileptic seizures based on semiology. Acta Epileptologica. 2019 Dec;1(1):1-5.

questions.question_text: Idiopathic progressive calcium deposition in the basal ganglia is seen in
questions.explanation: Fahr disease, also known as idiopathic basal ganglia calcification, is a rareautosomal dominant neurodegenerative disorder, characterised by bilateralcalcifications in multiple basal ganglia. Patients with Fahr disease may beasymptomatic or present with movement disorders such as parkinsonism,psychiatric disorders such as psychosis and depression, cognitive impairment,dementia, and a variety of other symptoms. The age on onset is mostly between 40and 50 years, but the symptoms can manifest at any age. Patients who becomesymptomatic early in adulthood mostly develop psychiatric or cognitive disorders,like psychosis, whereas patients who become symptomatic later in life developmainly movement disorders in combination with other clinical features.Ref: Peters ME et al. Mechanisms of calcification in Fahr disease and exposure ofpotential therapeutic targets. Neurology: Clinical Practice. 2020 Oct 1;10(5):449-57.

questions.question_text: Presence of which of the following should prompt investigations for a medicalcause of recurrent anxiety?

options.text: Onset of symptoms before the age of 25 years

questions.explanation: Once e!ective treatment has been adequately delivered and adhered to, there willbe a proportion of patients with anxiety that have not remitted and a smallerproportion that remain quite symptomatic. At this point, it should be consideredwhether there are exogenous factors that are aggravating and/or maintaininganxiety, whether there is a medical condition, and whether the diagnosis may bewrong or incomplete (i.e. whether there is a comorbidity present that is accountingfor the poor response to treatment).Ref: Roy-Byrne P. Treatment-refractory anxiety; definition, risk factors, andtreatment challenges. Dialogues in clinical neuroscience. 2015 Jun;17(2):191.

questions.question_text: What percentage of women with a history of schizophrenia will experience arelapse of psychosis within the first 12 months postpartum?
questions.explanation: Relapse of psychosis within the first 12 months postpartum occurs inapproximately 16% of women with a history of schizophrenia. This is less commonand manifests di!erently than in women with bipolar disorder.Ref: Meltzer-Brody S et al. Postpartum psychiatric disorders. Nature ReviewsDisease Primers. 2018 Apr 26;4(1):1-8.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is more indicative of HIV-associated vacuolar myelopathyrather than HIV-associated dementia?
questions.explanation: Because HIV-associated dementia (HAD) develops rapidly – over several weeks to afew months – it is considered a rapidly progressive dementia. Psychomotorretardation, loss of dexterity, and gait impairment are so characteristic that HAD isconsidered a prime example of subcortical dementia. HAD patients initially remainverbal and articulate. Later, reticence, apathy, and withdrawal predominate. Even inthe elderly, the rapidity of onset and presence of psychomotor retardation and gaitimpairment readily separate the clinical picture of HAD from Alzheimer disease.Vacuolar myelopathy is associated with advanced HIV infection. Patients presentwith ataxic gait, slowly progressive spastic paraparesis, dorsal column-type sensoryloss, incontinence, and erectile dysfunction. If HIV testing has not yet been done, itis important to consider HIV testing in patients with slowly progressive spasticparaparesis and/or progressive cognitive impairment.Ref: Kaufman DM, Geyer HL, Milstein MJ, Rosengard JL. Kaufman's ClinicalNeurology for Psychiatrists, 9 Edition. 2023. p. 134.Taylor DM, Gaughran F, Pillinger T. The Maudsley Practice Guidelines for PhysicalHealth Conditions in Psychiatry. 2021. p. 375. Asaduzzaman M et al. HIV-Associated Vacuolar Myelopathy and HIV-AssociatedNeurocognitive Disorder as an Initial Presentation in HIV Infection. Case Reports inInfectious Diseases. 2023 Jan; 1-7.

questions.question_text: The most common psychiatric symptom in Cushing syndrome is
questions.explanation: Cushing syndrome is a relatively rare but serious condition that results fromchronic hypercortisolism. Depression is the most prevalent and significantpsychiatric disorder among patients with Cushing syndrome.Ref: Lin TY et al. Psychiatric symptoms in Cushing's syndrome: a systematic review.Innovations in Clinical Neuroscience. 2020 Jan 1;17(1-3):30.

questions.question_text: Which of the following MRI findings is characteristically seen in Huntington disease?
questions.explanation: Huntington disease is a rare neurodegenerative disorder of the central nervoussystem, with a genetic autosomal dominant inheritance, that first involves the basalganglia (caudate nucleus and putamen) and results from expansion of a CAGtrinucleotide repeat in the HTT (huntingtin) gene. In Huntington disease, CT/MRIshow atrophy of the basal ganglia (caudate and putamen) with 'boxing' of thecaudate and dilatation of the ventricles.Ref: Bachoud-Lévi AC et al. International Guidelines for the treatment ofHuntington's Disease. Frontiers in neurology. 2019;10:710.Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019Jul 30. p. 166.

questions.question_text: Mr. Y has a history of depression and is about to receive treatment for multiplesclerosis. Which of the following medications should prompt prophylactictreatment with an antidepressant?
questions.explanation: The role of interferon-beta in the aetiology of multiple sclerosis (MS) depression isunclear, but it is now thought that depression occurs no more frequently in peopletreated with interferon-beta. Standard care for initiation of interferon-beta shouldinclude assessment for depression and, for those with a past history of depressiveillness, prophylactic treatment with an antidepressant.Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines inPsychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 808.

questions.question_text: A 45-year-old man with diabetes is brought to the emergency department withnausea, vomiting, lethargy, and muscle cramps. He has been diagnosed withdepression and recently started on fluoxetine. What is the most likely metaboliccomplication?
questions.explanation: Most antidepressants have been associated with hyponatraemia. The most likelymechanism of this adverse e!ect is the syndrome of inappropriate secretion ofantidiuretic hormone (SIADH). There is a strong level of supporting evidence thatSSRIs (including fluoxetine) are associated with a relatively high risk ofhyponatraemia. All patients taking antidepressants should be informed of andobserved for signs of hyponatraemia (dizziness, nausea, lethargy, confusion,cramps, seizures).Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines inPsychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. pp. 393-394.

questions.question_text: Of the following, which is most recommended for the treatment for post-strokedepression based on the best available evidence?
questions.explanation: Treatment of post-stroke depression is complicated by medical co-morbidities andby the potential for interactions with other co-prescribed drugs (especiallywarfarin). Contraindications to antidepressant treatment are more likely withtricyclics than with SSRIs. Fluoxetine, citalopram, and nortriptyline are probably themost studied and seem to be e!ective and safe. SSRIs and nortriptyline are widelyrecommended for post-stroke depression. Reboxetine (which, like nortriptyline,does not a!ect platelet activity) may also be e!ective and well tolerated, althoughits e!ects overall are doubtful. Vortioxetine may be of particular interest owing toits additional benefits on cognition (independent of e!ects on depressivesymptoms). It also does not appear to adversely a!ect cardiovascular parametersor interact with warfarin or aspirin, but there are currently no data to support itsuse specifically in post-stroke depression.Ref: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines inPsychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 362.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is appropriate to screen women for postpartum depression?
questions.explanation: The Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale is a 10-item tool developed for screeningpostpartum women for depression in outpatient clinics, home visits, or duringpostpartum appointments. Ref: Smith-Nielsen J et al. Validation of the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scaleagainst both DSM-5 and ICD-10 diagnostic criteria for depression. BMC psychiatry.2018 Dec;18(1):1-2.

questions.question_text: In ICD-11, which of the following is included under dissociative disorders?
questions.explanation: The ICD-11 divides ICD-10 possession trance disorder into the separate diagnosesof trance disorder and possession trance disorder. The separation reflects thedistinctive features in possession trance disorder wherein the customary sense ofpersonal identity is replaced by an external "possessing" identity attributed to theinfluence of a spirit, power, deity, or other spiritual entity. In addition, a greaterrange of more complex behaviours may be exhibited in possession trance disorder,while trance disorder typically involves the repetition of a small repertoire ofsimpler behaviours.Ref: Reed GM et al. Innovations and changes in the ICD-11 classification of mental,behavioural and neurodevelopmental disorders. World Psychiatry. 2019Feb;18(1):3-19.

questions.question_text: What is the untreated case fatality rate in patients with herpes simplex encephalitis?
questions.explanation: Before the use of acyclovir, the (untreated) case fatality rate of herpes simplex encephalitis was up to 70%. Although acyclovir administered intravenously has substantially improved outcomes for HSV encephalitis (mortality reduced from 70% untreated to 8% treated), 35% of those who survive still have long-term neuropsychiatric disabilities including cognitive and seizure disorders.Ref: Stahl JP, Mailles A. Herpes simplex virus encephalitis update. Current opinion in infectious diseases. 2019 Jun 1;32(3):239-43.Kapadia RK et al. Encephalitis in adults caused by herpes simplex virus. CMAJ. 2020 Aug 10;192(32):E919-.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a condition classified in ICD-11's new sexual health chapter?
questions.explanation: ICD-10 gender identity disorders have been renamed as 'gender incongruence' in ICD-11 and moved from the mental disorders chapter to the new sexual health chapter, meaning that a transgender identity is no longer considered a mental disorder. ICD-11 guidelines explicitly state that gender variant behaviour and preference alone are not sufficient for making a diagnosis of gender incongruence.ICD-11 paraphilic disorders include exhibitionistic disorder, voyeuristic disorder, pedophilic disorder, coercive sexual sadism disorder, and frotteuristic disorder.ICD-10 categories of sadomasochism, fetishism, and fetishistic transvestism have been eliminated.Ref: Reed GM et al. Innovations and changes in the ICD-11 classification of mental, behavioural and neurodevelopmental disorders. World Psychiatry. 2019 Feb;18(1):3-19.

questions.question_text: A 33 year old man has intractable seizures. Which of the following may support a diagnosis of psychogenic nonepileptic seizures rather than epileptic seizures?

options.text: Loss of body tone during a seizure

questions.explanation: Ref: Xiang X et al. Differential diagnosis between epileptic seizures and psychogenic nonepileptic seizures based on semiology. Acta Epileptologica. 2019 Dec;1(1):1-5.

questions.question_text: A 52-year-old patient in palliative care has both depression and co-morbid pain. Which of the following medications should be chosen for the treatment of her depression?
questions.explanation: In the setting of palliative care, no clinically significant differences in terms of efficacy have been shown amongst the most commonly used antidepressants. Given equivalent efficacy, an antidepressant should be chosen based on considerations of: (1) activating versus sedating features, (2) tolerability, and (3) potentially useful side effects or other indications of the antidepressant. It is recommended to choose escitalopram or sertraline for tolerability, duloxetine if there is co-morbid pain, duloxetine or bupropion if there is a melancholic presentation of depression, and methylphenidate if the patient is at the end of life.Ref: Riordan PA et al. Top ten tips palliative care clinicians should know about psychopharmacology. Journal of palliative medicine. 2019 May 1;22(5):572-9.

questions.question_text: MRI may show hypointensity of the striatum in patients with
questions.explanation: Fahr disease, also known as idiopathic basal ganglia calcification, is a rare autosomal dominant neurodegenerative disorder, characterised by bilateral calcifications in multiple basal ganglia. Patients with Fahr disease may be asymptomatic or present with movement disorders such as parkinsonism, psychiatric disorders such as psychosis and depression, cognitive impairment, dementia, and a variety of other symptoms. This variability in symptoms can partly be explained by the division of the basal ganglia into dorsal and ventral systems.The dorsal striatum plays a major role in motor and cognitive functions, whereas the ventral striatum plays a role in motivational functions. Calcifications in Fahr disease are present as high-density areas on CT scans but can be more difficult to detect with conventional MRI sequences in early stages. Calcified lesions can appear hypointense in T2-weighted images, because of the presence of other minerals in the same areas and the difference in the composition of calcium deposits, such as zinc, manganese, iron, and magnesium.Ref: Peters ME et al. Mechanisms of calcification in Fahr disease and exposure of potential therapeutic targets. Neurology: Clinical Practice. 2020 Oct 1;10(5):449-57.Donzuso G et al. Basal ganglia calcifications (Fahr's syndrome): related conditions and clinical features. Neurological Sciences. 2019 Nov;40:2251-63.

questions.question_text: 'Baby blues' are experience by up to what proportion of new mothers?
questions.explanation: Up to three-quarters of new mothers will experience a short-lived period of tearfulness and emotional lability, starting 2-3 days after birth and lasting 1-2 days, called 'baby blues'. This is easily recognisable by midwifery staff and requires only reassurance and observation towards resolution. There is weak evidence that it may relate to post-partum reductions in the levels of oestrogen, progesterone, and prolactin (which occur around 72 hours after birth).Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 494.

questions.question_text: Frequent medical visits, splitting of the treatment team, and high risk of iatrogenic harm are most associated with which of the following psychiatric conditions?
questions.explanation: In ICD-11, bodily distress disorder has replaced the somatoform disorders of ICD-10. Bodily distress disorder is characterised by the presence of bodily symptoms that are distressing to the individual and excessive attention toward the symptoms, which may be manifest by repeated contact with health care providers. Frequent medical visits and extensive interactions with the health care system often occur.There is a high risk of iatrogenic harm and iatrogenic substance dependence.Hostility and frustration can be felt on both sides of the doctor-patient relationship with splitting between members of the treating team.Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 864.International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems (11th ed. ICD-11; World Health Organization, 2020)

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements is incorrect about bodily distress disorder?

options.text: The most frequent symptoms are non-specific and atypical
It is associated with significant psychological distress and functional impairment
It usually presents before the age of 40
Symptoms are usually isolated to a single organ system
Patients usually have long, complex medical histories

correct_answer.text: Symptoms are usually isolated to a single organ system

correct_answers.text: Symptoms are usually isolated to a single organ system

questions.explanation: In ICD-11, bodily distress disorder has replaced the somatoform disorders of ICD-10. Bodily distress disorder is characterised by repeated presentations with medically unexplained symptoms, affecting multiple organ systems, first presenting before the age of 40 years. It is usually chronic in adults, and is associated with significant psychological distress, functional impairment, and risk of iatrogenic harm. Patients have long, complex medical histories, although at interview, they may minimise all but the most recent symptomatology. The most frequents symptoms are non-specific and atypical.Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 864.

questions.question_text: What percentage of patients will die by completed suicide in the 24 months after an initial act of self-harm?
questions.explanation: Roughly 1% of patients will die by completed suicide in the 24 months after an initial act of self-harm, with the risk highest in the weeks following the original act.This represents a mortality by suicide 50-100 times that of the general population.Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 848.

questions.explanation: Ref: Correia R, Jackson D. Risk to self: identifying and managing risk of suicide and self-harm. BJPsych Advances. 2021 Mar;27(2):126-36.

questions.question_text: Of the following, episodic panic attacks are reported most often in patients with
questions.explanation: Pheochromocytoma is a rare tumour of the adrenal gland that produces catecholamines. It often presents with a classic triad of headache, palpitations, and generalised sweating. Anxiety is the fourth most common symptom and may mimic panic attacks. Ref: Alguire C et al. Unusual presentation of pheochromocytoma: thirteen years of anxiety requiring psychiatric treatment. Endocrinology, diabetes & metabolism case reports. 2018 Apr 6;2018(1).

questions.question_text: Which of the following age groups are at increased risk of traumatic brain injury compared to the general population?
questions.explanation: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a common cause of death and lifelong disability(largely due to neuropsychiatric sequelae) in young adults. Common causes are road traffic accidents, falls, and assaults. Alcohol is often a contributory factor.Improved life expectancy has, however, led to an increase in TBI in the frail elderly in high-income countries, shifting the peak incidence from 20s to 40s.Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 172.

questions.question_text: The most common co-morbid psychiatric condition associated with hypochondriasis is
questions.explanation: Hypochondriasis has a particularly high co-morbidity with generalised anxiety disorder, over 50%. Hypochondriasis may also co-exist with major depressive illness, OCD, and panic disorder. Examination of the time course of symptom development and most prominent clinical features helps to distinguish primary hypochondriasis from a secondary clinical feature of these disorders.Ref: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press;2019 Jul 30. p. 870.

questions.question_text: Which lobe of the brain is most commonly affected in patients with herpes simplex encephalitis?
questions.explanation: Herpes simplex encephalitis causes amnesia accompanied by personality changes, focal impaired awareness seizures (previously named complex partial seizures), and the Kluver-Bucy syndrome because the virus typically enters the undersurface of the brain through the nasopharynx and preferentially attacks the temporal lobes. This condition occurs relatively frequently because herpes simplex is the most common cause of sporadically occurring (non-epidemic) viral encephalitis.Ref: Kaufman DM, Geyer HL, Milstein MJ, Rosengard JL. Kaufman's Clinical Neurology for Psychiatrists, 9 Edition. 2023. p. 112.

questions.question_text: Mrs. P su!ers from epilepsy and co-morbid depression. She has been tried on SSRIs with no benefit and is keen to try an older antidepressant. The safest choice in her case would be
questions.explanation: Moclobemide is not known to be proconvulsive. Most TCAs are epileptogenic at higher doses (particularly clomipramine and amitriptyline). Bupropion has a dose-related risk of seizures.Antidepressants in epilepsy:-       Low risk: SSRIs, mirtazapine, duloxetine-       Probably low risk: agomelatine, MAOIs, moclobemide, reboxetine, vortioxetine-       Moderate risk: lithium, trazodone, venlafaxine, vilazodone-       High risk: amoxapine, bupropion, maprotiline, TCAsRef: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 789.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is untrue with respect to investigations in herpes simplex encephalitis (HSE)?

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is the imaging of choice in HSE
Gold standard for in vivo diagnosis is CSF polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for herpes simplex virus
Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) examination commonly reveals a lymphocytosis and raised protein
The EEG is invariably abnormal in HSE
CT scan usually reveals signal change and swelling within the frontal lobes

correct_answer.text: CT scan usually reveals signal change and swelling within the frontal lobes

correct_answers.text: CT scan usually reveals signal change and swelling within the frontal lobes

questions.explanation: Brain abnormalities in herpes simplex encephalitis (HSE) may be visible on CT but are much more consistently seen on MRI with gadolinium. MRI is the most sensitive method of detecting early lesions and is the imaging of choice in HSE. Brain MRI typically shows hyperintensities involving the cortex and white matter in T2 and FLAIR images - areas of contrast enhancement can also be present. Gold standard for HSE diagnosis is cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for HSV which has a sensitivity and specificity of >95%. False negatives can occur in the first 72 hours of onset. Other supportive findings include CSF pleocytosis (increased lymphocytes) and raised protein, abnormalities on EEG, and brain lesions or enhancement involving the temporal lobe, orbitofrontal and/or insular cortex on MRI. The EEG in HSE is invariably abnormal. Non-specific slowing may be the only feature early in the illness; later stages are more likely to be associated with high voltage periodic lateralizing epileptiform discharges. If present, they are diagnostically useful, but are not specific for HSE. Ref: Stahl JP, Mailles A. Herpes simplex virus encephalitis update. Current opinion in infectious diseases. 2019 Jun 1;32(3):239-43.Kapadia RK et al. Encephalitis in adults caused by herpes simplex virus. CMAJ. 2020 Aug 10;192(32):E919-.

questions.question_text: Most cases of herpes simplex encephalitis are caused by
questions.explanation: Most cases of herpes simplex encephalitis (HSE) in adults are caused by herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) and occur equally in both sexes. Age >50 years is an important risk factor. HSE most frequently affects the medial temporal lobes, but can also affect the insular, cingulate, and frontobasal cortex.Ref: Stahl JP, Mailles A. Herpes simplex virus encephalitis update. Current opinion in infectious diseases. 2019 Jun 1;32(3):239-43.Kapadia RK et al. Encephalitis in adults caused by herpes simplex virus. CMAJ. 2020 Aug 10;192(32):E919-.
